R0: Rule for Distinguishing selection bias from sample representation: When evaluating arguments based on samples, determine if the flaw concerns how items were selected (selection bias - e.g., inspectors deliberately choosing items they suspect are defective) versus whether the sample fairly represents the whole (sample representation - e.g., assuming field inspectors were equally likely to choose defective and non-defective items without justification). Selection bias focuses on the selector's intent or method; sample representation focuses on statistical validity regardless of intent.
R1: Rule for Distinguishing specific instance fallacy from hasty generalization: A specific instance fallacy occurs when a single example is used to disprove a general claim (e.g., 'Last week's good turnout disproves the claim that they regularly can't attract audiences'). A hasty generalization occurs when a small or unrepresentative sample is used to support a broad conclusion (e.g., 'All students oppose the policy because those who attended the meeting were opposed'). The direction matters: specific-to-general is hasty generalization; using specific to refute general is specific instance fallacy.
